title: Economists Should Not Be In Charge
author: Peter Greene
summary: Peter Greene uses Cory Doctorow's critique of economists to argue that the philosophy of economism has distorted education policy for decades. He walks through five failings attributed to economists, namely overreliance on models, underreliance on data, a rejection of society, a failure to understand irrationality and ethics, and their own prejudices, and maps each onto education reform. Merit pay, high-stakes testing, value-added measures, market school choice and competency badges are all shown to rest on the assumption that people act only from self-interest. His closing move is to state what education is actually for, helping young people become their best selves and learn what it means to be fully human, and to call economism a cramped view of both schooling and life.
points: Economism treats people as slaves to incentives, which leads reformers to assume teachers can only be moved by bribes or threats such as merit pay.
High-stakes testing is an economist-style design that rewards unethical behaviour, from test-prep narrowing of the curriculum to outright cheating.
Market-based choice treats schools and teachers as atomized individuals and ignores that competition can weaken the shared system meant to support all students.
Reforms like value-added measurement and employer-priced skills treat schools as assembly lines and ignore the expertise of teachers who work with education data daily.
Greene's counter-claim is that education is about helping young people become fully human, a purpose no cost-benefit model can capture.
quotes: Most of us believe that we do stuff because we want to be good people, and that other people act the same. But the dominant political philosophy for the last half-century, "economism," views us as slaves to "incentives" and nothing more.

In education, we've been subjected to talk about the cold hard outputs of deliverables, based on a testing system whose validity is based on unicorn wishes and fairy dust. And, of course, the actual expertise of teachers who swim in education data daily has been dismissed and ignored.

Schools--both students and faculty--must be understood as atomized individuals, and the fact that unleashing market forces for some would weaken the system that is meant to support all is simply irrelevant. Economism is the principle of "I've got mine, Jack" as a guiding light.

But high stakes testing, a very economist approach to running education, incentivizes all manner of unethical behavior, from cutting meaningful education in favor of test prep all the way up to just plain cheating. And the notion that competing for merit pay would make schools function more poorly by stifling cooperation--that's just an unfathomable mystery to economics man.

Economism has permeated too much of ed reform in the past few decades, not just in assuming that the only rational approach is to pull the levers of self-interest, but in measuring everything based merely on its monetary measure. The notion of "value-added" measurements, as if schools are comparable to assembly lines cranking out toasters. The idea that education's goal is to give students skills whose worth is measured by a future employer's willingness to pay for them.
